passage:
For three years Kunal had been the first to arrive at the Pune office and the last to leave. He believed that if he did excellent work, somebody upstairs would notice. On a Monday in March, the promotion list went up, and it didn't have his name on it. It did have the name of a colleague who attended every leadership lunch.

That evening at a chai stall near the metro station, Kunal told Samir, an older friend from another firm, "I thought loyalty was enough."

Samir stirred his tea. "It's not nothing. But people can only vouch for what they've seen. Who has seen your work?"

Kunal thought about it. Nobody senior had, not really.

The next week he asked to present his supplier project at the monthly review, and he asked his manager to be his sponsor. It felt a little awkward. It also felt real.

qa.q: Where did Kunal talk to Samir?
qa.a: Kunal talked to Samir at a chai stall near the metro station.

qa.q: Why was Kunal so shaken when the promotion list went up?
qa.a: Kunal had believed that loyalty and hard work were enough to be rewarded and that someone upstairs would simply notice.

qa.q: What did Kunal do differently after the conversation?
qa.a: He asked to present his supplier project at the monthly review and asked his manager to sponsor him, so his work became visible to more senior people.

qa.q: How does Samir see the situation differently from Kunal?
qa.a: Samir sees loyalty as valuable but not self-advertising, since people can only support what they have seen, and he guides Kunal without becoming cynical.

grounding: Kunal learns that loyalty and hard work are not automatically rewarded, grieves the belief and learns about visibility and advocacy.

passage:
In the cooperative sugar mill's office outside Moga, Gurleen had kept the cane-weighing records spotless for five years. When the chief clerk retired, everyone told her the post was hers.
It went to Kiran, the general manager's nephew's friend, who played cricket with the directors on Sundays.
Gurleen walked home along the canal, kicking a stone. So it was all a game. Why bother?
Her old teacher, Harpreet-madam, stopped her at the gurdwara gate that evening. "Why so heavy?"
Gurleen told her. Madam listened. "It's unfair. But does the manager know what you've done? Or only that the records are fine?"
Gurleen was quiet. She had never once told anyone about the fraud she'd spotted in 2022.
The next month she wrote a short report on the year's work and asked Madam's nephew, a director, to read it. She still did the records perfectly. But now, people knew.

qa.q: Who got the chief clerk post?
qa.a: Kiran, the general manager's nephew's friend, who played cricket with the directors.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling on her walk home along the canal?
qa.a: She felt bitter and disillusioned, kicking a stone and wondering why she should bother after five years of careful work.

qa.q: How did Gurleen respond without giving up on effort?
qa.a: She kept the records perfect but also wrote a short report of her year's work and asked a director to read it.

qa.q: How might Harpreet-madam see Gurleen's situation?
qa.a: Harpreet-madam sees the unfairness but also that Gurleen's work has been invisible, and wants her to speak up rather than give up.

grounding: The protagonist learns hard work is not automatically rewarded and politics matter; she grieves, then learns visibility and advocacy without turning cynical.
